lesson.title: Hypomania and the Weight of Depression: Bipolar II Disorder
lesson.summary: Bipolar II disorder requires at least one hypomanic episode plus at least one major depressive episode, but never a full manic episode, making it easy to mistake for depression alone.
lesson.body:
Bipolar II disorder is often misunderstood as a milder version of bipolar I disorder, but it is more accurate to say it is built from a different pair of ingredients. Diagnosis requires at least one hypomanic episode (a noticeably elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy, lasting at least four days) together with at least one major depressive episode. Critically, the person must never have had a full manic episode. If a full manic episode ever occurs, the diagnosis becomes bipolar I disorder instead, regardless of how many hypomanic or depressive episodes preceded it. Hypomania shares the same broad symptom list as mania (elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, increased talkativeness, and so on) but it does not cause marked impairment in functioning, does not require hospitalization, and never involves psychotic features. It is a real, observable shift, just not a severe or dangerous one on its own.

This structure creates a genuine diagnostic trap. Depressive episodes tend to be the reason people seek help: they are painful, disabling, and hard to hide. Hypomanic episodes, by contrast, can feel good. A person may experience a stretch of unusually high energy, confidence, and productivity and simply think they are finally functioning well, not that anything is clinically notable. As a result, bipolar II disorder is frequently misdiagnosed as major depressive disorder, particularly when a clinician only hears about the depressive episodes and never asks about, or is never told about, the less distressing high periods. Recognizing hypomania as a distinct clinical entity, rather than dismissing it as simply a good week, is essential to getting the diagnosis and treatment right, since the two conditions are treated differently.

Because bipolar II disorder sits conceptually next to bipolar I disorder, comparing the two side by side is the clearest way to understand each: bipolar I is defined by the presence of full mania, with depression common but not required, while bipolar II is defined by the presence of hypomania together with major depression, and specifically by the absence of full mania. The next chapter looks closely at what elevates a hypomanic episode into a full manic one, since that line is exactly what separates these two diagnoses.
